overview.text: Fertilizer is a material added to soil or plants to supply nutrients and support growth, supplementing the nutrients already present in the soil. Many fertilizers provide nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K), which have different roles in plant growth. Fertilizers can be packaged blends or materials such as manure and compost; their nutrient content and how quickly plants can use those nutrients vary. In agriculture, supplying nutrients helps produce crops for food, feed, fiber, and fuel. Too much fertilizer can waste resources and harm the environment when nutrients move into waterways, so application should match plant and soil needs.

key_facts.text: Fertilizer labels commonly list N-P-K in that order; the numbers indicate the proportions of those nutrients in the product.
Nitrogen supports leaf growth, phosphorus supports roots and fruiting, and potassium helps plants stay hardy and resist disease.
Manure and compost can supply nutrients; many organic nutrient sources must be broken down by soil organisms before plants can use them.
Commercial fertilizer is a major source of nutrients applied to crops, but manure and other organic materials can also contribute nutrients.
Applying more nutrients than plants need can harm the environment; fertilizer choices and amounts should be guided by soil and plant needs.
